column4: Today, you can see a number over everyone's head. It counts every lie they've told today.
Mo's coffee is fine. It is not the best.
Most of the numbers are tiny. And then there's Pip.
Thirty-seven. It's seven thirty-one in the morning.
By midnight, you'll know why. And you won't like your own number.
Rule one. It counts every lie, big or small.
Rule two. It resets at midnight.
Rule three. Nobody else can see it.
You check the whole island. Zero. Zero. Zero.
In one survey of a thousand American adults, about six in ten said they hadn't told a single lie that day.
So who is Pip lying to?
In that same survey, half of all the lies came from about five people in every hundred.
A few people tell most of the lies. And today, one of them is Pip.
By the afternoon, everyone you love is lying to you. And without this power, you'd never know.
People catch a lie only about fifty-four percent of the time. Barely better than flipping a coin.
Every lie today was hiding the same thing.
In one diary study, about one in four everyday lies was told for someone else's sake.
Even honest people have bad lie days.
And there, in the window, is your own number. Twelve.
Best ever. On my way. I'm not mad.
People in that study said they didn't think their lies were serious, and barely worried about getting caught.
Researchers who reviewed decades of lie studies suggest we judge other people's lies more harshly than our own.

You'll never see anyone's number. But in a study that followed people's lies for three months, almost nine in ten lies were little white lies, and people said lies were only about seven percent of everything they said. So believing people is usually a safe bet. And the next time you're about to tell a little one, just notice it.
Everyone tells a few. Most people, most of the time, are telling you the truth.
